digest.top_line: ASTRO BCC/cSCC guideline: definitive RT graded strong for non-surgical pts; PORT strong for cSCC adverse features (T3-T4, PNI, uncorrectable margins), only conditional for BCC equivalents.
digest.tldr: A guideline-heavy day: all consensus documents, no new outcome data. Skin carries the most RT weight: ASTRO grades PORT by histology, GEC-ESTRO ACROP sets BT technique by depth (contact <5 mm, interstitial ≥5 mm). IMWG favours BKP/PV over RT for myeloma VCF pain, RT reserved for soft-tissue mass. UK COVID lung guidance compresses 55Gy/20 to 52Gy/15 fx.

sites.intro: Two consensus documents, neither backed by RCTs: both state their schedules rest on retrospective or experience-based data.

studies.tldr: Consensus technique guide for skin BT: contact BT for tumours <5 mm deep, interstitial for ≥5 mm or curved surfaces; no single standard schedule recommended.

verdict.rationale: Society recommendations, not an outcome study. Evidence base is single-institution small series with no randomised data; dose schedules explicitly experience-based. Changes technique and margin standards, not efficacy claims.
verdict.audience: NMSC (BCC, SCC, Merkel) and keloids considered for skin brachytherapy

studies.significance: The dosimetric traps are the actionable content: a missing applicator cap raises skin dose 2.5x (Valencia) to 10x (Leipzig), Valencia surface dose runs ~135% at a 3 mm prescription, and interstitial catheters shallower than 3 mm risk necrosis. The 5 mm depth threshold, set by HF ultrasound, decides contact versus interstitial technique.
studies.monday_clinic: In an elderly or frail pt with a small NMSC under 5 mm deep on a flat surface, this supports contact BT with a shielded applicator over interstitial technique; it does not extend to lesions ≥5 mm thick or on curved facial surfaces, which fall to interstitial implants.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: GEC-ESTRO ACROP **consensus recommendations** (Radiotherapy and Oncology, 2018) covering technique, margins, dose and planning for skin BT. Panel composition and consensus method are **not described in source**.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Non-melanoma skin cancer (BCC, SCC, Merkel cell), plus keloid prophylaxis. Special-site sections cover nose and ear, eyelid, extremities, and frail elderly pts.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Contact BT (moulds, flaps, shielded applicators) for tumours **<5 mm deep**; interstitial for **≥5 mm** thickness or irregular surfaces. Interstitial HDR/PDR runs **2.5-4 Gy per fraction twice daily**; LDR **60 Gy** at the 85% isodose. Shielded applicators prescribe to **3-4 mm** with a **1-2 mm** PTV margin for setup.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: Catheters must sit **≥3 mm** under skin to avoid telangiectasia, necrosis or delayed healing. Lower-limb sites carry poor healing risk and increased fractionation is advised. For the eyelid, minimum bolus of 0.5 mm above and 1 mm below the shield neutralizes backscatter.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Positions BT against surgery rather than as its replacement: surgery remains the eyelid gold standard, with interstitial BT for cases where function cannot be preserved. Cites an ABS summary of **19 protocols** with local control of **90-100%**, and nasal vestibule HDR BT matching surgery on locoregional control with better cosmesis.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents BCC, SCC and Merkel cell skin primaries and post-excision keloids treated with HDR, PDR, LDR or electronic BT. Does not represent melanoma or nodal disease.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Table 2 schedule data could not be row-attributed in the extracted text. Device content is 2018 vintage: Valencia VH4/VH5 were under development and the AAPM/ESTRO TG-253 QA guidance was still in progress. BED is called unhelpful for comparing surface schedules of differing duration.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The value is technical standardization (depth-based technique choice, histology-based margins, cap and source-to-skin distance rules) rather than a dose standard. The authors decline to fix a schedule and ask for **surface dose to be recorded** so outcome-toxicity correlation becomes possible.

studies.interpretation:
This document belongs in the category of practice consolidation, not evidence generation. Its own conclusions concede the point: skin brachytherapy rests on single-institution series of modest size, with no randomised trials, systematic reviews or meta-analyses to anchor it. What the panel can credibly standardize, then, is geometry and physics, and that is where the recommendations are firmest. The decision rule that most often matters in clinic is depth: contact techniques for tumours under 5 mm, interstitial implants for thicker lesions or curved surfaces such as the face. That threshold is driven by dose falloff from a surface source, which is why the document pushes high-frequency ultrasound to define depth rather than relying on clinical palpation.

The dose-fractionation section reads differently. The authors list several schedules per applicator and then state plainly that prescriptions rest more on experience than evidence, and that BED is a poor tool for comparing surface schedules of differing overall time. A reader should take the schedule list as a menu of accepted practice, not a ranking. The single firm dose statement is historical: for LDR interstitial work, escalating beyond 60 Gy added cosmetic harm without proportionate control gain. For HDR contact work, nothing comparable exists, which is why the panel asks centres to record skin surface dose. That request is the most forward-looking line in the paper, because surface dose, not prescription-depth dose, is what plausibly drives late cosmesis, and with a Valencia applicator the surface sits around 135% of a 3 mm prescription.

The physics warnings deserve more weight than their placement suggests. Omitting the plastic cap on a Leipzig or Valencia applicator multiplies skin dose by roughly 10 and 2.5 respectively, an error that is easy to make and invisible on a library plan. Many users still plan these applicators by hand calculation or library plan without CT data, so the cap check and applicator immobilization are the real quality safeguards.

Against surgery, the document is measured. It accepts surgery as the eyelid gold standard and frames BT as the option when function or cosmesis cannot be preserved, citing nasal vestibule data showing similar locoregional control with better aesthetic outcomes. The ABS summary it references, with local control of 90-100% across 19 protocols, supports efficacy in selected, largely elderly series, but these are not comparative data and selection almost certainly flatters them.

What would make the guidance wrong is a prospective dataset showing that surface dose, fraction size, or the hypofractionated schedules offered to frail pts carry more late toxicity than the series suggest. The margin table, borrowed partly from surgical SCC guidance, is also an assumption that has not been tested for brachytherapy specifically. Until such data exist, this is a sound technical reference with an evidence base its authors openly call thin.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: The dosimetric traps are the actionable content: a missing applicator cap raises skin dose 2.5x (Valencia) to 10x (Leipzig), and Valencia surface dose runs ~135% at a 3 mm prescription. The 5 mm depth threshold, set by HF ultrasound, decides contact versus interstitial technique.

Does recorded skin surface dose predict late cosmesis?

verdict.rationale: ASTRO practice guideline; recommendations graded mostly low-to-moderate QoE from retrospective and single-arm series, with no RCT comparing RT vs surgery.
verdict.audience: Non-metastatic invasive BCC/cSCC, definitive or postoperative curative RT

studies.significance: Nodal dose is the most transferable read: 6000-6600 cGy after lymphadenectomy, 5000-5400 cGy elective, and the panel found no data supporting 6600 cGy for positive margins or extranodal extension. Elective nodal RT is conditional, reserved for cSCC >6 mm thick when the primary field already overlaps the basin, which narrows routine nodal coverage.
studies.monday_clinic: In resected cSCC with uncorrectable close/positive margins, T3/T4 disease, or desmoplastic/infiltrative histology under immunosuppression, this supports PORT as a strong recommendation; for BCC with the same margin or recurrence features, support is only conditional.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: ASTRO clinical practice guideline: **5 key questions**, systematic MEDLINE review (May 1988 to June 2018), modified Delphi consensus. Strength of recommendation is graded **separately from quality of evidence**.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Adults with **non-metastatic invasive BCC or cSCC** treated with curative-intent RT. Excluded re-irradiation, palliation, preclinical and dosimetric studies.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Primary site: definitive **BED10 70-93.5** (conventional) or **56-88** (hypofractionated); postoperative **59.5-79.2** or **56-70.2**. Nodal: **6000-6600 cGy** adjuvant after lymphadenectomy, **5000-5400 cGy** elective. Gross perineural spread treated to definitive doses, preferably conventional fractionation.

analysis_sections.label: Regimen
analysis_sections.body: Concurrent carboplatin with adjuvant RT for resected cSCC is **not recommended** (Strong). Concurrent drugs with definitive RT for unresected locally advanced cSCC are **conditionally recommended** (Low QoE).

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: The only randomized cutaneous evidence cited is a **negative** trial of weekly carboplatin added to PORT in high-risk resected cSCC. Adjuvant cisplatin chemoRT benefit comes from mucosal H&N SCC trials and was not extrapolated to skin.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents adults with non-metastatic invasive BCC or cSCC of the head and neck, trunk, or limbs receiving curative-intent RT. Does not represent metastatic disease, re-irradiation, palliation, or mucosal H&N, vulvar, penile, or perianal SCC.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Trunk and limb recommendations are **extrapolated** from head and neck series. **Microscopic perineural invasion** is left without a recommendation, and BED10 ranges are wide by design rather than schedule-specific.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: Strong grades here usually reflect panel certainty on benefit vs harm, not trial-level proof. The carboplatin recommendation stands, but the KQ5 position on cemiplimab as palliative-only **predates C-POST and neoadjuvant cemiplimab data** and reads as dated.

studies.interpretation:
The useful way to read this document is as a codification of practice that grew up without trials. The panel states plainly that no randomized study compares surgery with RT for BCC or cSCC, and the grading reflects it: the strong recommendations mostly sit on moderate evidence, and the dose-fractionation recommendations sit on low evidence while still being graded strong. That combination is legitimate under ASTRO's system, which separates strength from quality of evidence, but a reader should register that strong here usually means panel confidence that benefit outweighs harm, not trial-level proof. The KQ4 BED10 ranges are wide by design, an attempt to accommodate the heterogeneous schedules of a retrospective literature rather than an endorsement of any single schedule.

The most decision-relevant feature is the asymmetry between cSCC and BCC after surgery. The same indications (close or positive margins that cannot be corrected by re-excision, recurrence after a margin-negative resection) earn a strong recommendation for cSCC and only a conditional one for BCC, consistent with the panel's view that cSCC carries far greater regional and nodal risk. Gross perineural spread is the one PORT indication shared at strong strength across both histologies. Microscopic perineural invasion, which is where much of the day-to-day ambiguity in clinic actually sits, gets no recommendation and is relegated to future research.

On regional disease the guideline is more conservative than some practice. Clinically apparent nodes go to lymphadenectomy plus adjuvant RT, with a carve-out for the single small cervical node without extracapsular extension, and definitive nodal RT is reserved for inoperable or unresectable disease. Elective nodal RT is conditional and tied to field overlap with the primary, an expert-driven compromise reached after the panel considered and then dropped a recommendation against routine elective treatment. The adjuvant nodal dose argument, that 6000 cGy suffices and that escalation for positive margins or extranodal extension lacks data, is extrapolated from mucosal head and neck series rather than cutaneous evidence.

KQ5 is where the document has aged most. The one randomized cutaneous trial it cites, weekly carboplatin added to PORT in high-risk resected cSCC, was negative, and the recommendation against that combination is sound. But the position that cemiplimab and hedgehog inhibitors are palliative agents to be avoided where curative surgery or RT is feasible predates the neoadjuvant cemiplimab experience and the C-POST adjuvant trial. A reader applying KQ5 today should treat it as a statement about carboplatin, not as current guidance on immunotherapy around RT.

What would make the rest wrong is mainly selection. The evidence base comes from series of pts chosen for RT, predominantly head and neck, with trunk and limb recommendations explicitly extrapolated. The local control and cosmesis claims for definitive RT are credible but not comparative, so the conditional recommendation for function- or cosmesis-sparing RT appropriately rests on shared decision-making rather than demonstrated equivalence with surgery. The guideline's own scheduled reaffirmation window has also passed, which is a further reason to check for a successor before treating KQ5 as current.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Nodal dose is the transferable read: 6000-6600 cGy adjuvant after lymphadenectomy, 5000-5400 cGy elective, with no data supporting 6600 cGy for positive margins or ENE. Elective nodal RT is conditional and tied to field overlap with the primary, narrowing routine nodal coverage.
significance_by_specialty.medonc: The one randomized cutaneous trial cited was negative for weekly carboplatin with PORT, so concurrent carboplatin after resection is a strong recommendation against. Concurrent drugs with definitive RT for unresected cSCC are only conditional on low QoE, and the cemiplimab stance predates adjuvant and neoadjuvant IO data.
significance_by_specialty.surgonc: Clinically apparent nodes go to therapeutic lymphadenectomy plus adjuvant RT, except a single <3 cm cervical node without ECE; definitive nodal RT is reserved for inoperable or unresectable disease. Close/positive cSCC margins not correctable by re-excision earn strong PORT support, BCC only conditional.

studies.significance: The usable lever is the radiobiology: with α/β 10, 52Gy/15 fx is isoeffective for tumour control, and with α/β 3, 50Gy/15 fx is isotoxic to 55Gy/20 fx for late complications. That conversion is what lets a department drop five fractions from a 20-fraction course, but it is modelled equivalence, not observed outcome.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Peripheral SABR: consider **30Gy to 34Gy in a single fraction**. Moderate hypofractionation: **52Gy/15 fx** isoeffective for tumour control (α/β 10); **50Gy/15 fx** isotoxic to 55Gy/20 fx for late complications (α/β 3).

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: Cited chest wall toxicity: **30.6%** for lesions abutting the chest wall, **8.2%** for tumours ≤1 cm from it, overall grade ≥3 chest wall toxicity **1.4%**. For lesions >5cm, OAR constraints must be met as when treating lesions ≤5cm.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: The 5-fraction option leans on RTOG 0813 dose constraints; 50Gy in 5 fractions has been used in Glasgow on that basis.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents pts receiving curative-intent lung RT during the COVID-19 pandemic. Does not represent palliative lung RT.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Most of the PDF text layer is font-encoded, so the per-setting schedule grid and size cutoffs could not be read. Cited toxicity figures come from other series whose regimens are not legible here.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The document is a bridge, not a result: it converts existing schedules into shorter ones using α/β modelling and borrowed constraints. Whether those compressions hold up on observed toxicity and control was not settled by the guidance itself.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: The α/β conversions (52Gy/15 fx for tumour control at α/β 10; 50Gy/15 fx isotoxic to 55Gy/20 fx at α/β 3) are the transferable piece for compressing a 20-fraction course. Single-fraction SABR at 30Gy to 34Gy carries the chest wall caveat: 30.6% toxicity cited for lesions abutting the wall.

studies.monday_clinic: In MM with a painful VCF and no intracanal soft-tissue mass, this questions RT as the pain treatment in favour of BKP/PV; it does not extend to soft-tissue compression with neurological deficit, where steroids, chemo and immediate RT stay first.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: IMWG consensus statement updating the **2008** recommendations on vertebral cement augmentation in MM. Panel process (voting, agreement, evidence grading) is **not described** in source.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: MM pts with VCFs, split at the first decision point by **presence or absence of neurological deficit**. MRI (sagittal STIR and T1) confirms a painful fracture; CT assesses stability and soft tissue vs bone in the canal.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: RT for local control and palliation should be used **judiciously and sparingly** to spare marrow. It shrinks soft-tissue mass but does not treat bony compression or stabilise the fracture. **Prior RT and its dose are not contraindications** to BKP/PV; cord compression without neurological deficit may not need RT.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: CAFE randomised **134 cancer pts, 49 with MM** (22 BKP vs 27 NSM) and favoured BKP on pain, function and QoL. The sham-controlled osteoporotic trials (Kallmes, Buchbinder) found **no benefit vs sham**, which the panel attributes to excluded high-need pts and facet-related pain.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents MM pts with painful VCFs, with or without neurological compromise. Does not represent solid-tumour spinal metastases, which the panel flags as possibly a different clinical problem.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Myeloma-specific randomised data are limited to a **49-pt subset** of one trial. The claim that kyphoplasty beat additional RT for pain rests on a single citation with no figures given. RT guidance carries **no dose, fractionation or target volume**.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The statement reorders spinal management around **systemic therapy first, bracing as a bridge, cement for persistent fracture pain**, and fixation avoided because of weak bone and infection risk. The panel itself names NSM vs VP vs BKP comparison and optimal timing as **unanswered RCT questions**.

studies.interpretation:
This is an IMWG update of its 2008 statement, and its operative recommendation is simple: MM pts with significant pain at a fracture site should be offered BKP or PV within 4-8 weeks unless medically contraindicated. For a radiation oncologist the more consequential content is what the document does to RT's role in the myeloma spine. The panel draws a clean mechanistic line: RT is effective against a soft-tissue myelomatous mass, ineffective against bony neural compression, and does nothing to stabilise a fractured vertebra. Combined with a call to use RT judiciously and sparingly to preserve marrow, and a prediction that rapidly acting systemic combinations should reduce the need for palliative RT, the statement effectively moves the painful, stable, mass-free VCF out of the RT clinic and into the procedural one.

The evidence underneath that shift deserves scrutiny. The myeloma-specific randomised data amount to the MM subset of CAFE, 49 of 134 cancer pts, with 22 allocated to BKP and 27 to non-surgical management. Everything else is observational series and osteoporosis literature. The two sham-controlled osteoporotic trials, Kallmes and Buchbinder, were negative, and the panel discounts them on selection grounds and on the argument that enrolled pts may have had facet-joint pain rather than fracture pain. That argument is plausible, but it is argument, not data, and the asymmetry matters: the negative evidence is the blinded evidence, the positive evidence is unblinded, and pain is the endpoint where blinding counts most. The statement that additional kyphoplasty outperformed additional radiation or systemic therapy for pain relief is cited to a single reference without any magnitude in the text, so an RT reader cannot judge how large the gap is or what RT regimen it was measured against.

The parts most directly usable in RT practice are the boundary conditions. Prior RT, and the dose previously delivered, are explicitly not contraindications to cement augmentation; the procedure runs through stab incisions, so wound-healing concerns do not apply. A pt treated with steroids, RT and chemo for soft-tissue cord compression can still be augmented later for persistent fracture pain or relative instability, with planned augmentation 4-8 weeks later or after the second chemo cycle. The panel also states that cord compression without neurological deficit may not need RT at all, on the basis that chemo and steroids resolve the soft-tissue mass. That is the claim with the largest potential effect on RT referral volume, and it arrives without supporting figures in the text.

What the document does not give is equally useful to know. There is no dose, fractionation or target-volume guidance, so the instruction to spare marrow has to be operationalised by the reader. There is no description of how the panel reached agreement and no grading of recommendation strength, so the absolute, relative and conditional tiers cannot be weighted by evidence quality. The panel itself lists head-to-head comparison of NSM, VP and BKP, and optimal timing in MM, as questions for a prospective randomised trial, and notes radiofrequency ablation with cement as still under investigation. The recommendation would be wrong if a blinded myeloma-specific trial reproduced the sham-controlled null; until then it is a reasonable expert framework resting on a thin randomised base.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: RT is narrowed to soft-tissue disease: effective against intracanal myelomatous mass, ineffective for bony compression, and it does not stabilise the VCF. Prior RT and its dose do not contraindicate cement, so irradiating a level leaves BKP/PV open 4-8 weeks later.
significance_by_specialty.medonc: Systemic therapy is framed as the most important modality: augmentation follows 1-2 cycles if fracture pain persists, coordinated with the haematologist to avoid cytopenias, with peri-procedural antibiotic prophylaxis. Bisphosphonates may add spinal stability via bridging bone, a hypothesis the panel flags for research.

The role of cement augmentation with percutaneous vertebroplasty and balloon kyphoplasty for the treatment of vertebral compression fractures in multiple myeloma: a consensus statement from the International Myeloma Working Group (IMWG)
papers.abstract: Abstract Multiple myeloma (MM) represents approximately 15% of haematological malignancies and most of the patients present with bone involvement. Focal or diffuse spinal osteolysis may result in significant morbidity by causing painful progressive vertebral compression fractures (VCFs) and deformities. Advances in the systemic treatment of myeloma have achieved high response rates and prolonged the survival significantly. Early diagnosis and management of skeletal events contribute to improving the prognosis and quality of life of MM patients. The management of patients with significant pain due to VCFs in the acute phase is not standardised. While some patients are successfully treated conservatively, and pain relief is achieved within a few weeks, a large percentage has disabling pain and morbidity and hence they are considered for surgical intervention. Balloon kyphoplasty and percutaneous vertebroplasty are minimally invasive procedures which have been shown to relieve pain and restore function. Despite increasing positive evidence for the use of these procedures, the indications, timing, efficacy, safety and their role in the treatment algorithm of myeloma spinal disease are yet to be elucidated. This paper reports an update of the consensus statement from the International Myeloma Working Group on the role of cement augmentation in myeloma patients with VCFs.
